title: What is an ETF?
subtitle: Exchange-traded fund - trades like a stock, diversifies like a fund
openingQuestion: How does an ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund) differ from buying individual stocks one by one?
openingOptions: An ETF is a basket of many assets, traded as one unit on the exchange
ETFs are only for institutional investors
An ETF only ever holds one single type of asset in the whole basket at once
explanation: An ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund) is a fund holding a basket of assets (stocks, bonds, commodities...) but traded on the exchange exactly like a single stock - it can be bought or sold at any time during the trading session. An ETF combines the diversification benefit of a fund with the liquidity and flexibility of a stock.

diagram.label: Traded on the exchange like a stock

realWorldExample.company: SPY - the ETF tracking the S&P 500
realWorldExample.description: SPY is the oldest and largest ETF tracking the S&P 500 index, letting an investor indirectly own the 500 largest US companies with a single buy order, at an extremely low management cost.

quiz.question: Why do ETFs usually have a much lower expense ratio than traditional mutual funds?
options: Because most ETFs track an index so they don't need a research team
Because ETFs are subsidized by the state specifically to encourage long-term passive investing
Because ETFs don't have to pay custody fees on the underlying assets
Because ETFs only hold a small number of stocks so they are easier to manage
quiz.explanation: Most ETFs passively track an existing index (S&P 500, VN30...), so they don't need a research team picking stocks the way active funds do - this sharply cuts operating costs. The creation/redemption mechanism through market makers also makes ETFs more tax- and cost-efficient than traditional mutual funds.

quiz.question: What problem can an ETF tracking a low-liquidity index run into, compared with one tracking the S&P 500?
options: A wide bid-ask spread and a price that drifts away from net asset value
It is not allowed to list on a stock exchange
Its management fee gets pushed higher than a traditional mutual fund's, since fewer market makers compete
It cannot be traded intraday and must wait until end of day
quiz.explanation: An ETF's liquidity depends heavily on market maker activity and the liquidity of the underlying assets - an ETF tracking a less popular index can have a wide bid-ask spread and a larger premium/discount to NAV, a real risk investors need to weigh beyond the expense ratio.

quiz.question: Where does an ETF differ from a mutual fund in how it trades?
options: An ETF requires a minimum one-year holding period before it can be sold
An ETF can only be bought from the fund management company, not through an exchange
An ETF trades intraday, while a mutual fund is priced once at the end of the day
An ETF does not allow individual investors to trade it
quiz.explanation: A mutual fund matches at a single price once a day based on net asset value. An ETF trades like a stock, so it can be bought or sold at any moment - convenient, but also easy to overtrade.

quiz.question: What mechanism keeps an ETF's price close to its net asset value?
options: Investors get refunded if the price deviates by more than five percent
The fund management company must publish a mandatory price each session
The exchange caps the ETF's daily trading band
Market makers trade to capture the spread
quiz.explanation: When an ETF trades above its true value, a market maker creates additional fund units and sells them to capture the spread, pushing the price back down. This mechanism only works well when the underlying assets are liquid enough.

quiz.question: Why did corporate bond ETFs run into trouble during liquidity crises?
options: Because the underlying bonds stopped trading, so the reference price lost its footing
Because investors were not allowed to sell the ETF during the crisis
Because the ETF's management fee spiked sharply once the market got volatile and illiquid
Because bond ETFs are forced to convert to cash when the market falls
quiz.explanation: In March 2020, many bond ETFs traded well below their published net asset value - because that value was based on bonds that had stopped trading. An ETF being more liquid than the assets it holds is a contradiction that only shows up when markets get stressed.

keyTakeaways: ETF: a fund holding a basket of assets but trading as flexibly as a single stock
Combines a fund's diversification benefit with a stock's liquidity
Usually has a much lower management fee than a traditional mutual fund

practicePrompt.question: You want to invest in a basket of 30 blue-chip stocks at once, but instead of buying each stock individually, you buy a fund certificate that can be bought or sold at any moment during the trading session, exactly like a single stock, with a price that changes continuously with supply and demand. What is this type of fund called?
options: This is called a Mutual Fund, priced and traded only once a day based on NAV
ETF: a fund holding a basket of assets but trading continuously intraday like a stock
This is called a Hedge Fund, a private fund type that is flexible and lightly regulated
This form of investing does not actually exist on real stock markets
practicePrompt.explanation: ETF: a fund holding a basket of assets but trading as flexibly as a single stock. This is a major advantage of ETFs over traditional mutual funds - combining diversification (many stocks in one fund) with high liquidity (continuous intraday trading like a stock).

summary.keyIdea: ETF: a fund holding a basket of assets but trading as flexibly as a single stock
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Combines a fund's diversification benefit with a stock's liquidity

application.title: Find an ETF that fits you
application.message: Look up an ETF trading on an exchange (domestic or foreign) in a theme you care about, and see what basket of assets it holds and how much its management fee is.
application.secondary: Looking it up yourself keeps the ETF concept from staying abstract.

sections.text: An ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund) is a fund holding a basket of assets - stocks, bonds, commodities - but traded on the stock exchange exactly like a single stock, buyable or sellable at any moment during the session. An ETF combines a fund's diversification benefit with a stock's liquidity and flexibility.
Why ETFs are usually cheaper than mutual funds

Most ETFs are passive funds tracking an index, so they don't need an expensive research team picking stocks the way active funds do. Add the creation/redemption mechanism through market makers, and ETFs are usually more tax- and cost-efficient than traditional mutual funds. SPY, the ETF tracking the S&P 500, lets an investor indirectly own the 500 largest US companies with a single buy order at an extremely low management cost.
The liquidity risk of small ETFs

An ETF tracking a less liquid index can have a wider bid-ask spread, and its exchange-traded price can drift meaningfully from the fund's actual net asset value (NAV), due to a lack of active market maker participation. This is a real risk to weigh alongside the expense ratio when choosing an ETF.
